notes.b: Food spoils because micro-organisms (bacteria, yeasts and moulds) and enzymes (natural proteins in the food that break it down) keep working. Heat processing stops both, and a clean airtight container then keeps new micro-organisms out.
points: Heat destroys vegetative bacteria (bacteria in their active, growing form), yeasts and moulds, and denatures (permanently changes the shape of) the enzymes that cause spoilage, so the food stops breaking down.
Sealing the food in a clean airtight container while it is hot, or sealing before heating, prevents re-contamination, because otherwise new micro-organisms would simply re-enter after the heating.

Spores (tough resting forms) of some bacteria, such as Clostridium botulinum, are very heat-resistant and survive boiling at normal pressure, so low-acid foods need higher temperatures held for longer, in a pressure cooker or retort (a large industrial pressure cooker).

Acid foods such as fruit, tomatoes and pickles are easier to preserve by heat because acid hinders micro-organisms and their spores. Low-acid foods such as peas, beans, meat and fish need a higher temperature.
Heat also changes the colour, texture, flavour and nutritive value of food, which is why heat-processed fruit and vegetables differ from fresh produce.
Heat-sensitive, water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C and the B group) are reduced by heat processing.
notes.tip: Matching and true/false questions ask you to name methods that use heat: jam, chutney, canning, bottling, pasteurisation and sterilisation. Learn all six.

notes.b: Heat treatments differ in how much they kill. A mild treatment leaves some organisms alive so the food must be chilled, while a severe one kills everything so the sealed food keeps at room temperature.
points: Pasteurisation is a moderate heat treatment that destroys most food poisoning (pathogenic) bacteria and reduces spoilage organisms, but not all spores, so pasteurised products keep for a limited time and still need refrigeration.
Milk is pasteurised at 72 °C for 15 seconds, then cooled rapidly. Pasteurisation is also used for cream, fruit juice, beer and some canned foods.

Sterilisation uses a higher temperature for longer, for example milk sterilised in the bottle and canned foods. It destroys all micro-organisms including spores, so the sealed product can be stored at room temperature.
The price of sterilisation is that flavour and colour change and vitamin losses are greater than with pasteurisation.
UHT (ultra-heat treatment) heats milk to about 135 °C for a few seconds, and the milk is then packed aseptically (in a germ-free way) into sterile cartons.
UHT milk keeps for months unopened at room temperature, must be refrigerated after opening, and has a slight cooked flavour.
Three processing methods make milk safe: pasteurisation, sterilisation or UHT, and evaporation or dehydration (drying).
notes.tip: Pasteurisation does not sterilise. It leaves some organisms and spores, which is why pasteurised foods are chilled, whereas UHT and canning sterilise. Exams on milk ask for three processing methods.

notes.b: Canning seals food in a container and heats it hard enough to sterilise it, so it keeps for a long time without a fridge. Commercial canning in tin cans is different from home bottling in glass jars.
points: Commercial canning has stages: food is prepared (washed, peeled, trimmed, blanched where needed), packed into cans, covered with brine, syrup or oil, and air is removed (exhausting).
Then the can is sealed with a double seam, heated in a retort at a high temperature for a set time, and cooled quickly. The heat sterilises the contents and the sealed can prevents re-contamination.
Cans are lined with a lacquer, a protective coating, to prevent the metal reacting with the food.
Canned food is shelf-stable, so it keeps at room temperature for a long time without refrigeration, and it can be eaten straight away.
Foods suited to canning include fruit, tomatoes, vegetables such as peas and beans, fish (tuna, sardines, salmon), meat, soup and baked beans.

Low-acid vegetables such as peas, beans and carrots must be processed in a pressure canner (a sealed pot that heats above 100 °C), because boiling water at normal pressure, which is 100 °C, does not destroy Clostridium botulinum spores.

A bulging can end or lid indicates gas produced by micro-organisms. Hissing, leaking, rust, deep dents or an off smell are also warning signs, so the contents must be discarded unopened and never tasted.
notes.tip: Keep canning (commercial, in a can, using a retort) separate from bottling (home, in glass). Commercial canning uses a retort at high temperature.

notes.b: The very high temperature and long processing time that make canned food safe also change it. Examiners ask what is lost and what is gained.
points: Vitamin C is heat-sensitive and water-soluble, so it is lost during high-temperature canning, especially into the canning liquid.
Thiamine (vitamin B1) is unstable at high temperature and is reduced by canning.
Canned vegetables are softer, paler and less bright in colour than fresh or frozen produce, and the flavour changes too.
Canned vegetables gain sodium from added salt (brine), so no-added-salt versions are preferred on a low-salt diet.
Fruit canned in heavy syrup gains sugar, and food packed in oil gains fat, which raises the energy content.
Heat destroys micro-organisms and enzymes in the can, which is the purpose of canning. Minerals and fibre are largely kept, and the liquid can be used in cooking to keep the nutrients it holds.

One past-paper table showed vitamin C in peas falling from 25 mg per 100 g fresh to 8 mg canned, and sodium rising from 1 mg to 230 mg. The reasons were the very high temperature and long time, and the salt used in canning.
notes.tip: For effects of canning, give water-soluble vitamin loss, changes in colour, texture and flavour, micro-organisms and enzymes destroyed, and added sugar, salt or fat from syrup, brine or oil. The 2021 question paired canning with dehydration. For data on peas, give the high temperature and long time for the vitamin loss, and added salt for the sodium.

notes.b: Bottling is the home version of heat preservation. Fruit is heated in glass jars so that the contents are sterilised and sealed.
points: Bottling packs fruit (and tomatoes) into clean sterilised glass jars with sugar syrup or water, seals them, and heats them in a water bath (or oven) until the contents reach a temperature that destroys organisms and enzymes.
The seal closes as the jar cools and a vacuum forms, which holds the lid down and keeps new micro-organisms out.
Jars must be filled hot, leaving headspace, and sealed at once; the contents cool and form a vacuum that holds the lid down.
Jars must be sterilised and undamaged with new or sound lids, and filled leaving headspace (a gap at the top). Hot jars must be lifted carefully.
Label bottled food with the date and store it in a cool, dark, dry place. Discard any jar whose lid is not tight or domed.

Low-acid vegetables and meat should not be bottled in a boiling-water bath at home, because boiling at normal pressure does not destroy Clostridium botulinum spores. They need pressure processing, so home bottling is restricted to fruit and acid foods.
Fruit is routinely bottled in a water bath because acid foods are easier to preserve by heat.
notes.tip: Sterilising jars is a hygiene step. Never call it pasteurising the jars. Home bottling of vegetables is not recommended without pressure processing.

notes.b: Jam is fruit boiled with sugar until it sets. It keeps because of heat, a high concentration of sugar and a sealed jar, and it sets because pectin, acid and sugar combine.
points: Heat: boiling at about 100 °C or higher destroys micro-organisms and inactivates enzymes in the fruit. The fruit is first simmered gently to soften its tissues and release pectin.
Sugar preserves by osmosis: at high concentration it draws water out of microbial cells, so they cannot multiply. Sugar also helps the gel to form and gives sweetness.

Pectin is a natural gelling substance, a carbohydrate found in the cell walls of fruit, mostly in the skin and core. It forms a gel with sugar and acid as the jam cools, so the jam sets. Pectin is not a preservative.

Apples, blackcurrants, redcurrants, gooseberries and lemons or other citrus fruit are high in pectin. Strawberries, raspberries, cherries and pears are low, so add pectin-rich fruit or a commercial pectin.

Acid, from lemon juice or the fruit itself, releases pectin from the cell walls and helps the pectin set. It also improves colour and flavour, and lemon juice is added for low-acid or low-pectin fruit.
Choose just ripe, firm, sound fruit. Under-ripe fruit contains more pectin, whereas over-ripe fruit has less pectin and spoils the set.
Sealing: pour the jam hot into clean sterilised jars and cover at once so micro-organisms cannot re-enter. A vacuum forms as the jam cools, and a waxed disc plus cover is the traditional method.
Jam loses some heat-sensitive vitamin C in boiling, its sugar concentration is high, and its flavour and colour change, so it no longer tastes fresh.
notes.tip: For principles of jam making, give each principle with its effect: heat destroys micro-organisms and enzymes, sugar draws water out by osmosis, pectin and acid make it set, and sealing prevents re-entry. Do not say sugar kills bacteria by heat, or that acid alone preserves the jam.

notes.h: Making jam: stages, setting point and spoilage
notes.b: A jam method runs in a set order, and each stage protects either the set or the keeping quality. Jam spoils when one of these protections fails.
points: 1. Wash and sterilise the jars, and prepare the fruit. 2. Simmer the fruit in a heavy pan to soften it and release pectin.
3. Add the sugar in the correct proportion, with lemon juice if needed, and dissolve it fully before the mixture is boiled rapidly to setting point.
Setting point is confirmed by the wrinkle test: a spoonful of jam dropped onto a cold saucer wrinkles when pushed with a finger. A sugar thermometer reads about 105 °C (220 °F) at setting point.
4. Skim the scum from the surface with a clean dry spoon. 5. Pot the jam into hot sterilised jars, seal at once, label and store in a cool, dry place.
Jam ferments or grows mould if too little sugar is used, setting point is not reached, jars or lids are not sterilised, the seal fails, or a dirty or wet spoon introduces yeasts and moulds.
Storage in a warm or damp place also spoils jam. Mould on the surface or fermentation (bubbles and an alcoholic smell) is the result.
notes.tip: A 25-mark account of jam making expects the full sequence: sterilise jars, prepare fruit, simmer, add sugar and possibly lemon, boil to setting point, test, skim, pot hot, seal, label, store. Method questions also ask why jam spoils. Do not confuse jam, which sets with pectin, with chutney, which is boiled with vinegar, sugar and spices.

keyTerms.definition: A moderate heat treatment that destroys most food poisoning bacteria in a food, but not all spores, so the food still needs chilling.
Heat treatment at a high temperature that destroys all micro-organisms, including spores.
Sealing food in a can or jar and heat-processing it so that it can be stored for a long period.
Preserving fruit or vegetables in sealed jars by heat processing them in a water bath or pressure canner.
A natural gelling substance found in the cell walls of fruit that causes jam to set when combined with acid and sugar.
The stage in jam making at which the mixture has boiled enough for pectin, acid and sugar to form a gel on cooling.
The gap left between the food and the top of a jar or container to allow for expansion and the formation of a vacuum.
A low-pressure space that forms inside a jar as hot contents cool, pulling the lid down and keeping air out.
A food poisoning bacterium that forms heat-resistant spores, which must be destroyed by pressure canning in low-acid foods.
A change in the three-dimensional structure of an enzyme or protein caused by heat, which destroys its activity.

factCards.term: Three effects of canning on vegetables
factCards.definition: Loss of vitamin C and thiamine (B1), an increase in sodium from added salt, and changes to colour, texture and flavour.

Pasteurisation destroys most food poisoning bacteria but not all spores, so the product must be chilled; sterilisation destroys all micro-organisms including spores, allowing room-temperature storage when sealed.

factCards.term: Four faults that lead to spoiled jam
factCards.definition: Too little sugar, setting point not reached, a faulty seal, and unsterilised jars or a contaminated spoon.

Why low-acid vegetables need a pressure canner

questions.prompt: Explain how canning changes the nutritional value of peas.
questions.model: Canning uses high temperatures for a long period, so heat-sensitive vitamin C is destroyed and thiamine (vitamin B1) is reduced. Vitamin C is water-soluble, so some is also lost into the canning liquid. Salt added to the can increases the sodium content.

questions.prompt: Give an account of how jam is made at home, explaining the underlying principles that preserve the jam and make it set.
questions.model: Method: sterilise the jars; prepare the fruit; simmer it in a heavy pan to soften it and release pectin; add the correct proportion of sugar and dissolve it; boil rapidly to setting point, tested with a cold saucer; skim the scum; pot into hot sterilised jars; seal at once; label and store in a cool, dry place. Principles: boiling destroys micro-organisms and inactivates enzymes; sugar preserves by osmosis, drawing water out of microbial cells; pectin, acid and sugar form the gel; the sealed jar prevents re-entry of micro-organisms.
